one_liner: Single-header C directory traversal library; faster than `find`, TinyDir, Cute Files, and Python os.walk on recursive walks.
what_it_does: CPath is a single-header C89/C99 filesystem-traversal library for listing/recursing directories on Windows and POSIX, written to avoid requiring C++17's std::filesystem. It exposes a C API built around one `cpathGetNextFile` loop (instead of separate hasNext/getFile/moveNext calls) plus a lightweight C++ wrapper (`cpath::Dir`/`File`, using `Opt<File, Error::Type>`) for pre-C++17 compilers. It is not a drop-in for `find`, `os.walk`, or `std::filesystem` — callers rewrite traversal code against CPath's own API.
how_it_is_fast: It does not eagerly call stat() on each entry; size/time info is loaded only on demand via `cpathGetFileInfo`, cutting per-entry syscalls versus TinyDir/Cute Files which stat every entry unconditionally. Its 'open file' (get file info from a path) needs a single syscall, versus TinyDir's approach of reopening and rescanning the parent directory (up to O(n) syscalls). The benchmark shows CPath and `find` have near-identical user time but CPath has much lower system time, consistent with the syscall-count reduction being the source of the win rather than faster CPU-bound logic.
when_to_use: Cross-platform (Windows + POSIX) recursive directory listing from C or pre-C++17 C++ without pulling in std::filesystem or Boost.Filesystem
You only need file names/types during traversal and want to skip stat() calls unless you actually need size/time
A small, vendorable single-header dependency (~2.5k lines, MIT) is acceptable in the build
Latency-sensitive walks over large trees where syscall count, not CPU work, dominates wall time
You're willing to pin to and self-patch an abandoned header if bugs surface
when_not_to_use: You need std::filesystem/Boost.Filesystem feature parity (symlink handling, watching, permissions, atomic ops) — the author explicitly states CPath is not a std::filesystem replacement
Windows-heavy usage: `cpathCanonicalise` has an open, unfixed length bug on Windows (issue #6), and CI never runs on Windows at all
You need active maintenance: master's last commit is 2019-09-28, and 7 issues opened in 2023 (including a real init bug) remain untouched
You need performance validated beyond one machine/toolchain: the only benchmark is first-party, single 2015 MacBook Air (dual-core i5 @ 1.6GHz), compiler unnamed, never independently reproduced
You need paths longer than a fixed stack buffer: paths are stored in fixed-size `CPATH_MAX_PATH_LEN` buffers, not dynamically sized (open issue #7 acknowledges this)

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C standard library (dirent.h/windows.h, sys/stat.h, stdlib.h, string.h, etc.)
integration.min_toolchain: C89/C99-era C; C++ bindings target pre-C++17 compilers (no C++17 required); CI builds with gcc on Ubuntu 16.04/latest and macOS 10.14/latest
integration.platforms: POSIX (Linux, macOS) and Windows in source (windows.h/tchar.h path exists), but CI only exercises Linux and macOS — Windows has an open, unresolved bug (issue #6) and is untested by CI
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no internal global mutable state was found in cpath.h, but the project makes no explicit thread-safety guarantee
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — requires rewriting traversal against cpathGetNextFile()/cpath_dir (C) or cpath::Dir/File with Opt<File, Error::Type> (C++), not a drop-in for find, os.walk, TinyDir, Cute Files, or std::filesystem

gotchas: cpathGetNextFile does not stat() automatically — call cpathGetFileInfo (File::GetFileInfo in C++) explicitly or size/time fields stay unpopulated
Open issue #1: the `file` output parameter isn't zero-initialized before a NULL check inside cpathGetNextFile — worth reading the source before relying on that check
Paths live in fixed CPATH_MAX_PATH_LEN stack buffers rather than growing dynamically; very long paths can fail rather than resize (open issue #7)
Windows cpathCanonicalise has a known, unfixed length-calculation bug (issue #6)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The siblings (FastReader, reckless) beat std::ifstream/fstream and stdio for reading/writing file contents and logging, a different problem than directory enumeration — there's no real overlap. Pick CPath only when the bottleneck is recursive directory listing itself; use FastReader for fast file reads or reckless for high-throughput logging.
verified_claims_summary: Averaged over 100 runs of a recursive traversal over a large synthetic directory tree (MacBook Air7,2, dual-core Intel i5 @ 1.6GHz, -O3, compiler unnamed), CPath (C or C++, recursion or emplace) measured 0.082-0.083s wall time versus 0.147s for GNU find, 0.237s for Python os.walk, 0.284s for Cute Files, and 0.294s for TinyDir — about 1.8x faster than find and roughly 3.4-3.6x faster than Cute Files/TinyDir (derived from the reported wall times). It was not benchmarked against std::filesystem.
status_note: Abandoned: master's last commit is 2019-09-28 (the raw repo pushed_at of 2023-09-24 reflects an unmerged side branch, not master); MIT-licensed and small enough (~2.5k-line single header) to vendor and patch yourself if needed.
